name: The Great Vowel Shift
statement: Between about 1400 and 1700 English long vowels all rose, which is why the spelling no longer matches the sound.
meaning: The Great Vowel Shift was a major series of changes in the pronunciation of English long vowels, taking place mainly between roughly 1400 and 1700, across the transition from Middle English to Early Modern English. All the long vowels were systematically raised, the tongue moving to a higher position, and the two already-highest long vowels turned into diphthongs. Because English spelling was becoming fixed by the printing press at the very time these pronunciations were shifting, the shift is the main reason modern English spelling diverges so sharply from how words are said. It transformed the sound of English into something close to its present form.
mechanism: Middle English had a set of seven long vowels, and the shift moved each of them. The mid and low long vowels were raised: the vowel of name went from an ah-like sound toward the modern ay, meet went from an eh-like long vowel toward ee, and boot rose toward oo. The two highest long vowels, unable to rise further, became diphthongs: the long ee of bite became the modern eye sound, and the long oo of house became the ow of now. Whether the changes formed a single coordinated chain, pushed or pulled along, or several independent shifts, and their exact ordering, remain debated.

examples.text: The long high vowels diphthongised: Middle English bite, once sounding like beet, became the modern eye sound, and house, once boo-se, became the ow of now.
The mid and low long vowels rose: meet went from an eh-like vowel to ee, and name from an ah-like vowel to the modern ay.
Printing, introduced to England by Caxton in 1476, fixed spellings reflecting older pronunciations just as the shift was under way, leaving English spelling famously irregular.

variants.name: Chain shift
variants.text: The model, associated with Jespersen, in which the vowels moved in a coordinated chain, with debate over whether higher vowels pulled the others up or lower ones pushed them.

variants.name: Several independent changes
variants.text: The alternative view that the long-vowel changes were structurally independent rather than one unified shift, with a distinct northern development.

whyItMatters: The Great Vowel Shift is the central event in the history of English pronunciation, separating the sound of Chaucer's English from Shakespeare's and from our own, and it is the leading reason English spelling is so notoriously inconsistent with speech. As a case study it is a showcase of systematic sound change and of the chain-shift idea in historical phonology, and it illustrates how the timing of a technology, printing, can freeze one layer of a language while another moves on. It remains a staple example in the study of how languages change.

working.text: read the shift as a coordinated raising of the long vowels, with the highest ones turning into diphthongs, not a scatter of isolated changes.
trace English spelling's irregularity to pronunciations shifting while printing was fixing the spellings that recorded the older sounds.
treat the causes and the exact chronology as unsettled, and the label itself as a modern coinage.

limits: The causes of the Great Vowel Shift are unknown, with no firm consensus; proposed factors include population movement after the Black Death, dialect and social contact, and hypercorrection. Whether it was a single unified shift or several structurally independent changes is debated, as is whether it was a push chain or a drag chain, and its exact chronology and ordering remain unclear after more than a century of study. It affected long vowels specifically, leaving short vowels largely untouched, and the very name is a modern label, coined only in 1909, not a term used at the time.
misreadings: The shift was gradual, unfolding over roughly three centuries, not a single sudden event. It concerns the long vowels specifically, so the short vowels were largely unaffected. Its causes are genuinely unsettled, so no single cause should be presented as established. And the Great Vowel Shift is a modern label, coined by Jespersen in 1909, not a term speakers of the period would have recognised.
origin: A series of sound changes in English long vowels between about 1400 and 1700; the term Great Vowel Shift was coined by the Danish linguist Otto Jespersen in the 1909 first part of his 'A Modern English Grammar on Historical Principles'.
